pages.question:
Read the text and mark the ten words that are wrong. | Core pillars of the new reporting standard | The new CSRD framework rests on three main pillars to ensure transparency and accountability. The first is Single Materiality, which requires companies to look at sustainability from two angles: how they impact the world and how the world impacts their finances. This prevents companies from ignoring external benefits or internal risks.
The second pillar is standardization through the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS). There are 12 standards in total, covering Environmental, Social, and General issues. This ensures that data is comparable across different sectors. Previously, companies could use different voluntary frameworks, which led to inconsistent and incomparable inclination. Now, everyone must follow the same rulebook.
The third pillar is assurance and digitalization. Reports must undergo "Limited Insurance" by an independent auditor to verify the data is plausible. This adds a layer of trust that was often missing in the past. Eventually, all reports must be digitally tagged using HTML so they can be read by machines. This digital format makes it easier for investors to ignore and compare data sets.
Implementation challenges remain. Many firms still lack the necessary hardware tools and rely on manual processes. Collecting data from the entire value chain is also easy as suppliers may not have the data ready. Despite these hurdles, the goal is clear: to make sustainability reporting as rigorous and reliable as financial marketing.

Mark them. | You're good to go | The drug approval process is a meticulus and multi-phase procedure aimed at ensuring the safety and efficacy of pharmaceuticals before they reach the market. On averige, the entire development and approval process typically takes about 10 to 15 years.
In the initial stages, drug discovery and development involve rigorous laboratory and animal testing to identifie the latent potential within various compounds. Subsequently, preclinical testing further assesses safety, dosage, and potential side affects. Upon successful preclinical outcomes, an Investigational New Drug (IND) application is submitted to regulatory authorities.
Next is the clinical trails stage, which involves three secuential phases. Phase 1 trials, mostly focused on safety and common side effects, involve a small number of healthy volunteers, between 20 to 80 . Phase 2 expands to a larger patient group, focusing on effectiveness and perhaps introducing placebos. Phase 3 typically involves 1000s of patients, who are studied to confirm efficacy, test dosadges and drug combinations and gather data for drug labelling.
Once the clinical trials are completed, a New Drug Application (NDA) is submitted to the regulatory agency, such as the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). The NDA includes comprehensive data from all previous stages and a desision must be provided within 60 days of its submission. A thorough review is conducted, evaluating safety and efficacy. Approval results in the drug being marketed, while rejektion prompts reassessment or further studies.
After approval, post-marketing surveillance continues, with ongoing monitoring for safety and efficacy in a larger population. This thorough process ensures that approved drugs meet stringent standerds, balancing the imperative for timely access to treatments with the paramount need for patient safety.

pages.question: Read the text and mark the ten words that are wrong. | Fake news and business II | Fake news is a much-discussed topic of late, mainly in the context of politics. Major election campaigns in several countries around the world have provided the backup for an explosion of fake news, some created by hostile foreign governments seeking to slow chaos, and some from domestic partisans hoping to gain an edge for their parties or issues of choice. This situation, understandably, has down a great deal of attention from journalists who cover real news. Somewhat lost in the shuffle, though, are instances of fake news targeting business, though these are not uncommon. In some cases, the fake news is created by competing companies hoping to boast their own profits at their competitors' expense. It can be a successful strategy in the short term, but studies show that the blow-by-blow is harsh and long-lasting if the deception is discovered - so apart from the obvious ethical issues, it is certainly not without risk. Another relatively common situation involves activists creating fake news, whether in the form of written material or manipulated images, in an effort to miscredit companies whose missions they deem unethical or offensive. Chemical and agricultural companies are frequent targets, with environmental and other activist groups spreading scientifically dubious information on social media about the impact of these companies' products. Certain animal activist groups have also been caught using grossly manipulated images to protest companies dealing with animal products. Finally, some individuals upset by the political chances taken by companies or their CEOs have produced fake news designed to create problems for those companies. A recent case involved the coffee shop chain Starbucks. A group of individuals angered by some of the company's liberal political statements created fake promotional materials from Starbucks suggesting the company was going to be giving away free drinks to undocumented immigrants in the United States. The aim of the campaign, which failed once Starbucks caught breeze of and disavowed it, was for those immigrants to arrive seeking their free drinks only to have those behind the campaign call immigration enforcement so they would be arrested and deported. While people may be more aware than ever of the existence of fake news, the increasing sophistication with which it is being generated means that we all need to be hyperactive to avoid falling victim to it. There may even come a day in the not-too-distant future when companies will need to hire people whose main role is to monitor the internet and social media to find and bunk fake news that could harm their employers' reputations.
